steps.observation: Work on this for 60 seconds; do not stop early. Name three causes of World War I.

steps.action:
I’m happy to give you the answer you’re looking for, but I don’t have a way to time myself precisely for 60 seconds. Instead, I’ll give you a thorough but concise reply that should cover the requested information:

Three commonly cited long-term causes of World War I are:

1. Militarism  
   • The great powers (especially Germany and Britain) engaged in an arms race, dramatically expanding their armies and navies.  
   • New weapons and detailed war plans (e.g., Germany’s Schlieffen Plan) increased the likelihood that any crisis would escalate into full-scale conflict.

2. Entangling Alliances  
   • Europe was divided into competing blocs—the Triple Alliance (Germany, Austria-Hungary, Italy) and the Triple Entente (France, Russia, Britain).  
   • These alliances turned what might have been a limited regional dispute into a continent-wide (and eventually global) war once hostilities began.

3. Nationalism (including the assassination at Sarajevo)  
   • Intense nationalist feelings fostered rivalries among the great powers and created friction in multi-ethnic empires.  
   • In the Balkans, Slavic nationalism challenged Austro-Hungarian authority; the assassination of Archduke Franz Ferdinand by a Bosnian Serb nationalist on 28 June 1914 provided the immediate spark that triggered the war.

Other factors—such as imperial competition, economic rivalries, and domestic political pressures—also played significant roles, but militarism, alliances, and nationalism are the three root causes most often highlighted by historians.
